route: Documented income earned in China (salary, fees, other current-account income)
use_it_when: The RMB is your own lawful income from China and you can show where it came from and that tax was dealt with.
limit: No amount ceiling in the rule. Tax evidence can be a tax payment certificate, an exemption certificate or the tax filing form; the tax filing rule covers single payments above USD 50,000.
advantages: The standard route for a foreign passport holder. One wire for the whole amount. Lowest bank cost of any conversion route.
drawbacks: The bank must see source documents and tax evidence. If tax was never paid on the income, it has to be settled first.
tax: No tax on the conversion itself in the sources read. Chinese income tax applies to the underlying income if it is still unpaid (3%-45% wages; 20% flat categories).

route: Change back unused RMB with the original exchange slip
use_it_when: You brought foreign currency into China, converted it to RMB less than 24 months ago, and still have the bank's exchange slip (兑换水单).
limit: Up to the unused amount shown on the slip; the slip is valid for 24 months from the exchange date. Without a slip: USD 500 a day.
advantages: Only your passport and the slip are needed. No income or tax documents.
drawbacks: Does not work for RMB earned or received in China, or for slips older than 24 months.
tax: None identified: this is your own money changed back.

route: Wire out foreign currency that is already in your Chinese foreign-currency account
use_it_when: Part of the balance is still USD (or another foreign currency), for example money wired in from abroad and never converted.
limit: For a foreign individual the rule names no amount threshold: remittance from the FX account is done on the passport. Unused inbound FX may be returned the way it came.
advantages: No conversion, so no exchange spread. Cheapest route: wire fee only.
drawbacks: Only helps for the part of the money that is already foreign currency. The bank still applies its own checks.

route: Proceeds from selling a home you owned in China
use_it_when: The RMB is what you received for selling residential property registered in your name.
limit: Not more than the sale price minus the taxes of that sale (your share if co-owned).
advantages: Handled directly by the bank with a fixed document list. Large amounts possible in one remittance.
drawbacks: Title transfer and tax payment must be complete first. The tax certificate amount caps what can be sent.
tax: Chinese income tax of 20% on the gain (sale price minus original cost and reasonable expenses). Other property taxes were not verified in this pass.

use_it_when: You are a foreign citizen who inherited assets in China from someone whose household registration was there.
limit: One application for the whole estate; after approval the bank may remit once or in instalments.
advantages: A dedicated legal route for large sums. Money goes straight to your own account in your country of residence.
drawbacks: Needs SAFE approval at the decedent's last hukou location, inheritance proof, property documents and a tax certificate. Takes preparation.
tax: A tax certificate from the tax office where the estate's property is located is required. No Chinese tax specific to inheritance was confirmed in this pass (flag U08). In the U.S., a foreign bequest above USD 100,000 is reported on Form 3520.

route: Emigrant property transfer (移民财产转移)
use_it_when: You used to live in mainland China, emigrated, and the assets were yours before you obtained emigrant status.
limit: One application for all the property to be moved; since 2014 the bank may remit once or in instalments within the approved amount.
advantages: A dedicated legal route for a former resident's savings and property proceeds. No annual quota.
drawbacks: Needs proof that the Chinese hukou was cancelled, an embassy-certified settlement certificate, property documents and tax certificates. Approval is at the former hukou location. Not available to someone who never had mainland residence.
tax: Tax certificates from the place where the property or income arose are required; any unpaid Chinese tax on that income or gain has to be settled.

route: Annual USD 50,000 convenience amount with a Chinese Foreign Permanent Resident ID
use_it_when: You hold the PRC Foreign Permanent Resident ID Card (not just a visa or residence permit).
limit: USD 50,000 equivalent per person per calendar year on the ID alone. Above it, the documented-income rule (L01) applies.
advantages: No source or tax documents inside the yearly amount.
drawbacks: Slow for large sums: USD 400,000 takes eight calendar years. A U.S. passport alone does not qualify.

route: Send the RMB itself abroad as cross-border RMB, convert outside the mainland
use_it_when: The RMB is lawful current-account income (the PBOC example is a foreign employee's salary) and your bank offers personal cross-border RMB remittance.
limit: Current-account income only. The bank's document requirements were not verified in this pass.
advantages: No onshore conversion step; the PBOC notes it saves the conversion charge in China.
drawbacks: You still have to convert RMB to USD at the receiving bank, at a rate and fee that are not officially published. Not every bank offers it to individuals.

route: Dividend from your own Chinese company
use_it_when: The money sits in a company you own, not in a personal account.
limit: Limited to genuine distributable profit. Above USD 50,000 the bank checks the profit-distribution resolution and the tax filing form.
advantages: The proper route for business profit; no annual quota.
drawbacks: 20% Chinese income tax on the dividend. Needs company accounts, a resolution and tax filing. Not a route for personal savings.
tax: 20% individual income tax on dividends. A lower treaty rate was not verified in this pass (flag U06). Tax paid in China may be creditable in the U.S.

route: Cash withdrawals abroad with a mainland UnionPay debit card
use_it_when: You have a UnionPay debit card on the RMB account and travel outside the mainland.
limit: RMB 10,000 per card per day and RMB 100,000 per person per calendar year across all cards.
advantages: No documents. Works for small amounts while travelling.
drawbacks: About 1.1% in card fees at Bank of China, before the exchange rate and the ATM owner's fee. USD 400,000 would take 27 calendar years. Exceeding the yearly cap suspends overseas withdrawals for that year and the next.
tax: None identified. Cash brought into the U.S. above USD 10,000 must be declared.

route: Carry foreign-currency cash out in person
use_it_when: You can lawfully buy the foreign currency first (L01, L02 or L07) and want it as banknotes.
limit: Up to USD 5,000 per trip without a permit; USD 5,000-10,000 with a bank-issued carrying permit; above USD 10,000 is in principle not allowed.
drawbacks: A delivery method, not a way around the document rules: the cash still has to be bought lawfully. Forty trips for USD 400,000. Theft and loss risk.
tax: None identified. Entering the U.S. with more than USD 10,000 (per family or group) requires FinCEN Form 105.

route: Using relatives' or friends' USD 50,000 amounts (splitting, 'ant moving')
drawbacks: SAFE treats it as evading the quota. The people involved go on the watch list for the year and the next two years; the organiser can be fined as 逃汇.
tax: Fine up to 30% of the amount, 30%-100% in serious cases; criminal liability possible.

route: Private swaps, money changers, apps, underground banks
drawbacks: Only banks and licensed exchange outlets may convert currency. 'I pay you RMB in China, you pay me dollars abroad' is private FX trading.
tax: Warning, confiscation of gains, fine up to 30%; 30%-100% in serious cases; criminal liability possible.

route: False documents or a false purpose to buy foreign currency
drawbacks: Buying FX with false or invalid documents is 非法套汇.
tax: Bank must reverse the conversion; fine up to 30%, 30%-100% in serious cases; untrue documents alone: up to RMB 50,000 for an individual.

route: Buying cryptocurrency or stablecoins with RMB to move value out
drawbacks: Exchanging legal tender for virtual currency in China is an illegal financial activity under the February 2026 notice.
tax: Activity is banned outright; funds have no legal protection.

route: Carrying more than USD 10,000 in cash out of China, or entering the U.S. without declaring it
drawbacks: Above USD 10,000 needs a SAFE permit that is in principle not granted. In the U.S., undeclared amounts over USD 10,000 can be seized.
tax: China: warning and fine up to 20% of the amount. U.S.: seizure and forfeiture, civil or criminal penalties.

route: Borrowing or lending bank cards to get around the overseas cash-withdrawal cap
drawbacks: Expressly forbidden by the 2017 SAFE notice.
tax: Punished under the Foreign Exchange Regulation.
